questions.prompt: What is a force?
questions.explanation: A force is simply a push or a pull on an object.

options: A push or a pull on an object

questions.prompt: In which unit is force measured?
questions.explanation: Force is measured in newtons (N).

questions.prompt: Forces always act in which way?
questions.explanation: Forces appear in pairs — one force in one direction, another in the opposite direction.

questions.prompt: What kind of force is the weight of an object?
questions.explanation: Weight is the downward pull of gravity, measured in newtons.

questions.prompt: What are balanced forces?
questions.explanation: Balanced forces are equal in size and opposite in direction, so they cancel out.

options: Equal and opposite forces that cancel out
Forces acting in the same direction

questions.prompt: When forces on an object are balanced, the object will:
questions.explanation: Balanced forces cause no change — the object stays still or moves at a steady speed.

options: Not change its state of rest or motion

questions.prompt: A book lies still on a table. The forces on it are:
questions.explanation: Weight down equals the normal force up, so the forces are balanced.

questions.prompt: A skydiver falls at a steady speed. This means:
questions.explanation: At steady speed, weight equals air resistance, so the forces are balanced.

options: His weight is greater than air resistance
The forces on him are balanced

questions.prompt: Newton’s first law says a moving object with no external force will:
questions.explanation: With no external force, a moving object keeps a steady speed in a straight line.

options: Keep moving at a steady speed in a straight line

questions.prompt: What are unbalanced forces?
questions.explanation: Unbalanced forces are unequal, leaving a resultant force that changes motion.

options: Unequal forces that leave a resultant force

questions.prompt: The resultant force is found by:
questions.explanation: Resultant = greater force − smaller force.

questions.prompt: A box weighs 50 N and air resistance is 20 N. The resultant force is:
questions.explanation: 50 N − 20 N = 30 N downwards, so the box falls.

questions.prompt: What are the two effects of unbalanced forces?
questions.explanation: They can start a stationary object moving and speed up a moving object.

options: Start motion / speed up in the direction of the resultant

questions.prompt: Two forces act on a box: 800 N right and 500 N left. The resultant is:
questions.explanation: 800 − 500 = 300 N to the right.

questions.prompt: The steady speed of a skydiver when forces are balanced is called:
questions.explanation: This steady balanced-force speed is the terminal velocity.

questions.prompt: Why does an object seem lighter in water?
questions.explanation: Upthrust from the water pushes up, so the object seems lighter.

questions.prompt: Upthrust on an object is equal to:
questions.explanation: Upthrust equals the weight of the displaced fluid (Archimedes’ principle).

options: The weight of the fluid it displaces

questions.prompt: A block displaces water weighing 10 N. The upthrust on it is:
questions.explanation: Upthrust equals the weight of water displaced = 10 N.

questions.prompt: What keeps a boat afloat?
questions.explanation: Upthrust from the displaced water balances the boat’s weight.

questions.prompt: Density is defined as:
questions.explanation: Density = mass ÷ volume (mass per unit volume).

questions.prompt: The formula for density is:
questions.explanation: Density = mass ÷ volume.

questions.prompt: An object of mass 200 g and volume 100 cm³ has a density of:
An object floats on water if its density is:
questions.explanation: Objects less dense than water float; denser ones sink.

questions.prompt: The density of water is about:
questions.explanation: Water’s density is about 1 g/cm³ (1000 kg/m³).

questions.prompt: Why do ships float higher in sea water than fresh water?
questions.explanation: Sea water is denser, so it provides greater upthrust.

options: Sea water is denser, giving more upthrust

questions.prompt: Why is it easier to float in the Dead Sea?
questions.explanation: High salt content makes it dense, giving greater upthrust.

options: Its high salt content makes it very dense

questions.prompt: Using the density table, which floats on water?
questions.explanation: Wood (900 kg/m³) is less dense than water (1000), so it floats.

questions.prompt: Which liquid is less dense than water?
questions.explanation: Petrol (800 kg/m³) is less dense than water.

questions.prompt: Pressure is:
questions.explanation: Pressure = force ÷ area.

questions.prompt: The formula for pressure is:
questions.explanation: Pressure = force ÷ area.

questions.prompt: The unit of pressure is the:
questions.explanation: Pressure is measured in pascals (Pa).

questions.prompt: A 100 N force acts on 2 m². The pressure is:
A 60 N box has a base of 2 m by 1 m. The pressure is:
questions.explanation: Area = 2 m²; 60 ÷ 2 = 30 Pa.

questions.prompt: For the same force, pressure is greatest when the area is:
questions.explanation: Small area gives high pressure for the same force.

questions.prompt: Pressure increases when the force is:
questions.explanation: For the same area, a larger force gives a larger pressure.

questions.prompt: Why is a person on a bed of nails not hurt?
questions.explanation: Large total area spreads the weight, giving low pressure.

options: Weight is spread over many nails, so pressure is low

questions.prompt: Why do stiletto heels damage floors?
questions.explanation: A tiny contact area gives very high pressure.

options: Small area gives very high pressure

questions.prompt: Why do football boots have studs?
questions.explanation: Studs reduce area, concentrating force so they cut into the ground for grip.

options: Small area concentrates force for grip

questions.prompt: Why do heavy trucks have wide tyres?
questions.explanation: Wide tyres increase area and lower the pressure so they don’t sink in.

options: To lower the pressure on the road

questions.prompt: Why do camels have wide feet?
questions.explanation: Wide feet spread weight, lowering pressure on the sand.

options: To lower pressure so they don’t sink in sand

questions.prompt: A sharp knife cuts better because it has:
questions.explanation: A thin edge gives high pressure, cutting easily.

questions.prompt: In a gas, the molecules are:
questions.explanation: Gas molecules are far apart and move fast in all directions.

options: Far apart and moving fast in all directions

questions.prompt: Why can air be squashed easily?
questions.explanation: Large gaps between molecules let a gas be compressed.

options: Its molecules are far apart with space between

questions.prompt: Atmospheric pressure is caused by:
questions.explanation: The weight of the air above, pulled by gravity, causes atmospheric pressure.

options: The weight of the air above pressing down

questions.prompt: Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about:
questions.explanation: About 100 kPa at sea level.

questions.prompt: Why are we not crushed by atmospheric pressure?
questions.explanation: The pressure inside our lungs and blood balances the outside air pressure.

options: Pressure inside our body balances it

questions.prompt: You can drink through a straw because:
questions.explanation: Sucking lowers the pressure inside; outside air pressure pushes the liquid up.

options: You pull the liquid with your teeth
Atmospheric pressure pushes the liquid up when you reduce pressure inside

questions.prompt: If a gas is squashed to half its volume (steady temperature), its pressure:
questions.explanation: Pressure × volume is constant, so halving volume doubles pressure.

questions.prompt: For a fixed gas at steady temperature, pressure × volume is:
questions.explanation: Pressure × volume stays constant (Boyle’s Law).

questions.prompt: Why does compressing a gas heat it up?
questions.explanation: Compression makes molecules move faster, raising the temperature.

questions.prompt: Pressure in a liquid is greatest:
questions.explanation: Pressure increases with depth, so it is greatest at the bottom.

questions.prompt: As you go deeper into a liquid, the pressure:
questions.explanation: More liquid above presses down, so pressure increases with depth.

questions.prompt: Pressure in a liquid acts:
questions.explanation: Liquid pressure acts in all directions.

questions.prompt: At the same depth, which exerts greater pressure?
questions.explanation: Denser liquids exert greater pressure; mercury is far denser than water.

questions.prompt: The pressure in a liquid depends on:
questions.explanation: Liquid pressure depends on depth and density, not the container’s shape.

questions.prompt: Why are dam walls thicker at the bottom?
questions.explanation: Pressure increases with depth, so the base must withstand the most pressure.

options: Water pressure is greatest at the bottom

questions.prompt: The pressure a liquid exerts on your body underwater is called:
questions.explanation: It is hydrostatic pressure, which increases with depth.

questions.prompt: Hydraulic machines transmit force using:
questions.explanation: Hydraulic machines use liquids to transmit force.

questions.prompt: Hydraulics work because liquids:
questions.explanation: Liquids barely compress and pass pressure equally throughout.

options: Are hard to compress and transmit pressure throughout

questions.prompt: A hydraulic jack is called a force multiplier because:
questions.explanation: A small input force produces a larger output force via the larger piston.

options: A small input force gives a large output force

questions.prompt: Input 12 N on 0.01 m², output area 0.1 m². The output force is:
In a car, the brakes work using:
questions.explanation: Pressing the pedal sends pressure through the brake fluid to the brake pads.

questions.prompt: Why can’t a gas be used in car brakes?
questions.explanation: A gas compresses instead of transmitting the pressure, making brakes spongy.

options: It compresses, so the brakes feel spongy
